edits.before: Strategy and credit. Everything rests on two elementary lemmas: an exact-separator characterization for a finite irredundant decomposition into pairwise incomparable primes (Lemma 3.1), and a contraction lemma that tests membership of a multihomogeneous component on its support by setting all other coordinates to zero (Lemma 4.2). The lower bound at the full-side primes P_{X} and P_{Y} (Propositions 5.1 and 5.2) is the substantive step: a separator of degree at most three is divisible by a product of two nonassociate irreducible quadrics, hence has degree at least four. The one-deleted-side bounds (Section 6) and the empty and mixed bounds (Section 7) are short support computations, and the lower bound is assembled in Theorem 7.3. Every quartic witness in Section 8 is an explicit construction of [3, Proposition 5.2], its published Q-case subscript slip being corrected here by direct verification; none of these ingredients is claimed as new. No determinantal quotient is ever assumed to be a unique factorization domain, and no characteristic is excluded. In keeping with the accompanying reviews, no worldwide-novelty or priority claim is made; the bounded qualification record is summarized in Section 11.

edits.before: Let I ⊆ S be a homogeneous ideal and P a minimal prime of I. The local v-number of I at P is v_{P}(I) = min{ d ≥ 1 : some homogeneous f ∈ S of degree d satisfies (I : f) = P }, provided this set is nonempty.
edits.after: Let I ⊆ S be a homogeneous ideal and P a minimal prime of I. The local v-number of I at P is v_{P}(I) = min{ d ≥ 0 : some nonzero homogeneous f ∈ S of degree d satisfies (I : f) = P }, provided this set is nonempty.

edits.before: By [1, Corollary 2.2] the ideal J_{G} is radical, and by [1, Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.9] its minimal primes are the ideals P_{T}(G) as T ranges over C(G), where for T with G_{V∖T} having connected components C_{1}, ..., C_{r} one takes P_{T}(G) to be L(T) together with, for each connected component C of the induced subgraph on V − T, the ideal of 2 x 2 minors supported on the completion of C to a clique. For the crown, every completion is a clique, so the general form specializes to the displayed ideals once the cut sets are known. The classification of cut sets is [3, Theorem 3.3]: for n ≥ 3 the nonempty T ∈ C(G) are exactly X; Y; X − {*a*_{i}}; Y − {*b*_{i}}; and the sets T = A ∪ { *b*_{c} : *a*_{c} ∈ A } with A ⊆ X, |A| = n − 2, whose complements are V − {*a*_{i}, *b*_{i}, *a*_{j}, *b*_{j}} for a pair i < j. The empty set occurs because G is connected, giving P_{0} = D(V); the mixed cut with deleted pair {i, j} gives M_{ij}. Each displayed ideal is prime: quotienting the L-part leaves a polynomial ring in the surviving variables and the block is the ideal of 2 x 2 minors of a generic two-row matrix, whose quotient embeds in a polynomial ring by the rank-one parametrization x_{w} = s t_{w}, y_{w} = u t_{w}; see also [1, Section 3]. Distinctness of the six families follows from their degree-one parts, which are L(T) for the six distinct deleted sets T (for P_{0} the degree-one part is zero, and 2n − 4 > 0 since n ≥ 4, so no mixed prime has empty L-part). As minimal primes of a radical ideal they are pairwise incomparable, and radicality identifies their intersection with J_{G} itself, not merely with its radical. Every vertex degree of the classification is strict for n ≥ 4, which is the only structural place the hypothesis n ≥ 4 enters; the full-side witnesses of Section 8 use it as well.

edits.before: Work componentwise (Lemma 4.1). A component whose support meets X lies in P_{X} = L(X) automatically. Consider a nonzero component h supported in U ⊆ Y. Since P_{Y}, all Q_{i}, all R_{i}, all M_{ij} and P_{0} are among the primes of (2) different from P_{X}, membership h ∈ Q_{i} for every i is available. By Lemma 4.2, h ∈ Q_{i} ∩ S_{U}, and the survivor ideal of Q_{i} in S_{U} is generated by the minors of D(Y − {*b*_{i}}) with both endpoints in U; there are none unless |U − {*b*_{i}}| ≥ 2.

edits.before: These two quadrics are irreducible and nonassociate in the polynomial unique factorization domain S_{U}, over any field. Indeed, as a polynomial in *x*_{*b*_{s}}, the minor [ *b*_{s}, *b*_{t} ] = *x*_{*b*_{s}}*y*_{*b*_{t}} − *x*_{*b*_{t}}*y*_{*b*_{s}} is linear and primitive: its coefficients *y*_{*b*_{t}} and −*x*_{*b*_{t}}*y*_{*b*_{s}} have no nonconstant common divisor, so Gauss’s lemma proves irreducibility. Nonassociation follows from the distinct vertex multidegrees of the two minors. Irreducible elements of this unique factorization domain are prime, and two nonassociate irreducibles are coprime; since both divide h, their product divides h. A nonzero multiple of that product has degree at least 4 > 3 = d, so h = 0. The coefficient pair is coprime in characteristic two as well, where − equals +; no sign or factoriality beyond the polynomial ring S_{U} is used, and in particular no unique factorization of a determinantal quotient. Hence every pure-Y component of f vanishes, the remaining components lie in P_{X}, and f ∈ P_{X}.

edits.before: Apply the symmetry that exchanges x with y and *a*_{i} with *b*_{i} for each index. It fixes J_{G}, P_{0} and each M_{ij}, exchanges P_{X} and P_{Y}, and exchanges Q_{i} with R_{i}; it preserves homogeneity and degree. The image of a preimage f under this symmetry satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 5.1 with P_{Y} in place of P_{X}, and the conclusion pulls back.
edits.after: Apply the symmetry that exchanges x with y and *a*_{i} with *b*_{i} for each index. It fixes J_{G}, P_{0} and each M_{ij}, exchanges P_{X} and P_{Y}, and exchanges Q_{i} with R_{i}; it preserves homogeneity and degree. Let σ denote this involution. Then σ(f) satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 5.1 for P_{X}; hence σ(f) ∈ P_{X}, and applying σ again gives f ∈ P_{Y}.

Its Lemma 5.7 treats the mixed cuts T = A ∪ { *b*_{c} : *a*_{c} ∈ A } with |A| = n − 2 through the identity v_{P_{T}}(J_{G}) = α((J_{G} : P_{T})/J_{G}), cited there from the colon-formula literature in the lineage of [7]; its proof compares two representations modulo J_{G}, a step the support argument of Section 7 avoids. edits.before: Two-component cuts over the complex numbers. Reference [4] works over C and its localized results require a minimal cut in the sense of its Definition 2.3: the deleted set leaves exactly two connected components. Its Theorem 4.15 applies to the crown cuts Q_{i}, R_{i} and M_{ij}, whose complements have two components: for Q_{i} a connected dominating set in the star component must contain *a*_{i} and two distinct *b*_{c}, *b*_{d} with c, d ≠ i, while the isolated component contributes *b*_{i}, giving 3 + 1 = 4; for M_{ij} each edge component contributes both endpoints, giving 2 + 2 = 4; R_{i} is symmetric. The full-side cuts P_{X} and P_{Y} instead leave n ≥ 4 singleton components, outside the two-component hypothesis; the general upper bound, Theorem 3.5 of [4], yields the localized value only under a radicality hypothesis on the colon that its proof does not extract from the degree of a transversal, and no transfer across fields is stated there. Thus [4] covers neither P_{X}, P_{Y} nor uniform positive characteristic.
edits.after: Two-component cuts over the complex numbers. Reference [4] works over C and its localized results require a minimal cut in the sense of its Definition 2.3: the deleted set leaves exactly two connected components. Its Theorem 4.15 applies to the crown cuts Q_{i}, R_{i} and M_{ij}, whose complements have two components. Under [4, Definition 4.6], the chosen vertices in each surviving component must form a connected dominating set in that component and also dominate the subgraph obtained by adjoining the deleted set T. For Q_{i}, the star-side choice must contain *a*_{i} and at least two distinct leaves *b*_{j}, *b*_{k}: with only *b*_{j}, the deleted *a*_{j} is undominated, while two distinct leaves dominate every deleted X-vertex. The isolated *b*_{i} also dominates all deleted X-vertices, giving 3 + 1 = 4. For M_{ij}, both endpoints of each edge are required to dominate deleted vertices on both sides, giving 2 + 2 = 4. The R_{i} case is symmetric. The full-side cuts P_{X} and P_{Y} instead leave n ≥ 4 singleton components, outside the two-component hypothesis; the equality case in Theorem 3.5 of [4] requires radicality of J_{G} + J_{transversal}, not radicality of the colon itself. Identifying that sum with the colon is the missing equality step; degree information about a transversal alone does not supply it. No transfer across fields is stated there. Thus [4] does not supply the full-side or uniform positive-characteristic result.
